name: Battle of Grunwald
info: The Polish and Lithuanian army under Władysław II Jagiełło and Vytautas defeated the Teutonic Order under Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen near Grunwald in 1410, killing him and much of the Order's leadership.

facts.place: Between the villages of Grünfelde (Grunwald), Tannenberg (Stębark) and Ludwigsdorf (Łodwigowo) in the Teutonic Order's territory, in present-day Poland; excavations of 2014 to 2019 placed the main battlefield about 2 kilometres south-west of the traditional site, south of Grunwald
facts.sides: The Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under King Władysław II Jagiełło and Grand Duke Vytautas, against the Teutonic Order under Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen; the contemporary sources give no reliable troop counts, and the high-end estimates of Stefan Kuczyński, 39,000 Polish and Lithuanian and 27,000 Teutonic men, are often cited in Western literature as commonly accepted
facts.outcome: The Teutonic army was defeated and Grand Master von Jungingen was killed, with much of the Order's leadership. The Order held out at Marienburg and lost little land in the Peace of Thorn of 1411, but it never recovered its former power.

t: No contemporary source gives reliable troop counts. Jan Długosz gave the number of banners: 51 Teutonic, 50 Polish and 40 Lithuanian, but it is unclear how many men were under each.

The Lithuanian light cavalry retreated after more than an hour of fighting. Długosz called it a complete annihilation of the Lithuanian army, while some historians propose a planned feigned retreat, and Stephen Turnbull argues that it did not quite fit that pattern.

The Order held out at Marienburg and lost little land at the Peace of Thorn, yet the indemnity it had to pay brought borrowing, higher taxes and unrest in its cities, and the Poles and Lithuanians were unable to turn the military victory into territorial gains.
dyk: The site of the battle was long placed in the wrong spot. Excavations between 2014 and 2019 found the main battlefield about 2 kilometres south-west of the memorial, and the mass graves found by the old chapel probably lie near the Teutonic camp.
ev: Jogaila of Lithuania agrees in the Union of Kreva to marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland, becomes Władysław II Jagiełło and creates a personal union of Poland and Lithuania
An uprising in Samogitia leads the Teutonic Order to declare war on Poland and Lithuania, and it invades Greater Poland and Kuyavia
A truce is signed in October, due to expire on 24 June 1410, and both sides prepare for war
The Polish and Lithuanian armies unite at Czerwińsk, cross the Vistula and enter Prussia in early July
The two armies fight between Grünfelde, Tannenberg and Ludwigsdorf, and Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen is killed
The main Polish and Lithuanian forces reach Marienburg in late July, and the siege is lifted on 19 September
Władysław II Jagiełło defeats the Order again in the Battle of Koronowo in October
The Peace of Thorn returns Dobrin Land to Poland, and the Order resigns its claims to Samogitia for the lifetimes of Władysław II Jagiełło and Vytautas

sections.background:
In 1230 the Teutonic Order, a crusading military order, moved to Chełmno Land and launched the Prussian Crusade against the pagan Prussian clans. It conquered and converted the Prussians by the 1280s, and then turned to the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania. For about 100 years it raided Lithuanian lands, particularly Samogitia, which separated the Order in Prussia from its branch in Livonia, but it gained very little territory.

In 1385 Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania agreed in the Union of Kreva to marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland. He converted to Christianity and was crowned King of Poland as Władysław II Jagiełło, creating a personal union between the two realms. Lithuania's conversion removed the religious rationale for the Order's activities, and the Order's grand master publicly contested the sincerity of the conversion. Samogitia had been in Teutonic hands since the Peace of Raciąż in 1404, and Poland had claims in Dobrzyń Land and Gdańsk. Trade also mattered: the Order controlled the lower reaches of the Neman, the Vistula and the Daugava.

In May 1409 an uprising began in Teutonic-held Samogitia. Lithuania supported it, and Poland announced its support for the Lithuanian cause. Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen declared war on 6 August 1409 and invaded Greater Poland and Kuyavia, catching the Poles by surprise. A truce signed on 8 October 1409, mediated by Wenceslaus, King of the Romans, was set to expire on 24 June 1410, and both sides used the time to prepare.
sections.forces:
The precise number of soldiers has proven difficult to establish, and none of the contemporary sources gave reliable troop counts. Jan Długosz gave the number of banners, the principal cavalry unit: 51 for the Teutons, 50 for the Poles and 40 for the Lithuanians. It is unclear how many men were under each banner, and the structure and number of infantry and artillery units is unknown. German historians tend to present lower numbers and Polish historians higher ones. The high-end estimates of Stefan Kuczyński, 39,000 Polish and Lithuanian and 27,000 Teutonic men, are cited in Western literature as commonly accepted.

The Teutonic army was outnumbered but had advantages in discipline, military training and equipment. Its heavy cavalry was noted, although few of its men were heavily armoured knights, and it had bombards. Soldiers from twenty-two states and regions, mostly Germanic, joined it. Both armies included mercenaries, primarily from Silesia and Bohemia, and Bohemian mercenaries fought on both sides.

Vytautas gathered troops from Lithuanian and Ruthenian lands, including three banners from Smolensk under Jagiełło's brother Lengvenis, a Tatar contingent of the Golden Horde and Armenian cavalry from Podolia. Jagiełło was overall commander but did not directly participate in the battle. Vytautas, second in command, led the Lithuanians and took part. Długosz said Zyndram of Maszkowice commanded the Polish army, which is highly doubtful; the marshal of the Crown, Zbigniew of Brzezia, more likely did.
sections.course:
The Polish and Lithuanian armies gathered at Czerwińsk and crossed the Vistula on a pontoon bridge between 24 and 30 June, marched north on 3 July and crossed the Prussian border on 9 July. Jagiełło chose on 11 July to bypass the fortified Drewenz crossing by turning east. Early on 15 July the armies met on about 4 square kilometres, on a north-east to south-west axis. The Teutonic army was ready first and hoped to provoke an attack. Its armoured troops stood in the sun for hours, and light rain dampened its powder, so that only two cannon shots were fired.

Vytautas, supported by Polish banners, attacked the Teutonic left flank. After more than an hour of heavy fighting the Lithuanian light cavalry began a full retreat. Heavy fighting then broke out between Polish and Teutonic forces. The Teutonic forces concentrated on the Polish right flank, and the royal banner of Kraków was lost and soon recaptured. Jagiełło committed his second and third lines, and von Jungingen led 16 banners, almost a third of the original Teutonic strength, to the Polish right. One knight charged the king, and his secretary Zbigniew Oleśnicki saved him.

The reorganised Lithuanians then returned and attacked von Jungingen from the rear. As he tried to break through the Lithuanian lines he was killed: Cronica conflictus says Dobiesław of Oleśnica thrust a lance through his neck, while Długosz names Mszczuj of Skrzynno. Surrounded and leaderless, the Order retreated. Part of the routed units fell back to their camp, where the camp followers turned against them. The battle lasted about ten hours.
sections.aftermath:
A note from envoys of King Sigismund of Hungary put total casualties at 8,000 dead on both sides, but the wording is vague and may mean 16,000. A papal bull of 1412 mentioned 18,000 dead Christians. Długosz listed only 12 Polish knights killed. According to Teutonic payroll records only 1,427 men reported back to Marienburg to claim their pay, and of 1,200 men sent from Danzig only 300 returned. Between 203 and 211 of the 270 brothers of the Order who took part were killed, among them the Grand Master, the Grand Marshal and ten komturs. Vytautas had Marquard von Salzbach and Heinrich Schaumburg executed after the battle.

Several thousand were taken captive, including Dukes Konrad VII of Oels and Casimir V of Pomerania. Most commoners and mercenaries were released on condition that they report to Kraków on 11 November 1410, and only those expected to pay ransom were kept.

The Polish and Lithuanian forces stayed on the battlefield for three days and reached Marienburg only on 26 July, which gave Heinrich von Plauen time to organise its defence. Many Teutonic fortresses surrendered, among them Danzig, Thorn and Elbing, but the besiegers suffered from lack of ammunition, low morale and dysentery, and the siege was lifted on 19 September. The Order recaptured most of the castles. Under the Peace of Thorn of February 1411 it ceded Dobrin Land and resigned its claims to Samogitia for the lifetimes of Jagiełło and Vytautas. It had to pay an indemnity in silver in four annual instalments, borrowed heavily and raised taxes; Danzig and Thorn revolted.
sections.sources:
There are few contemporary, reliable sources, and most were produced by the Polish. The most important is Cronica conflictus, written within a year of the battle by an eyewitness of uncertain identity; only a short 16th-century summary survives. Jan Długosz wrote his comprehensive account several decades later, and its reliability suffers from the gap and from his alleged bias against the Lithuanians. Banderia Prutenorum is a mid-15th-century manuscript with images of captured Teutonic flags. German sources include Johann von Posilge's chronicle. An anonymous letter discovered in 1963 gave details on Lithuanian manoeuvres.

Long thought to lie between the three villages, the site was placed south of Grunwald by Sven Ekdahl and by excavations of 2014 to 2017. At the old site, mass graves were found by the chapel ruins, with remains of more than 130 people in three pits and about 90 in the sacristy; Ekdahl believed the area was near the Teutonic camp. Only 28 artefacts connected with the battle were found in 1958 to 1990, and about 150 of 1,500 found by 2020 are linked to it. The surveys of 2014 to 2019 have been criticised for inconsistent publication.

The retreat of the Lithuanians is disputed. Długosz portrayed a Polish victory alone. Historians since Lastowski in 1909 have proposed a planned manoeuvre borrowed from the Golden Horde, and the German letter warned the new Grand Master against feigned retreats. Stephen Turnbull holds that it did not fit the formula, since a feigned retreat was usually staged by one or two units and followed swiftly by a counterattack.
sections.legacy:
The battle shifted the balance of power in Central and Eastern Europe and marked the rise of the Polish–Lithuanian union as the dominant regional force, and the Teutonic Order never recovered its former power. Unrest in Prussia led to the Prussian Confederation in 1441 and the Thirteen Years' War of 1454. Grunwald is regarded as one of the most important battles in Polish and Lithuanian history. In Lithuania it is synonymous with the Grand Duchy's peak, and in the age of Romantic nationalism it inspired resistance to Germanization and Russification. A monument by Antoni Wiwulski was unveiled in Kraków in 1910 before some 150,000 people. It is also commemorated in Ukraine and Belarus, and a re-enactment is held each 15 July.

In Germany the knights were generally seen as noble men who brought Christianity and civilisation to the east. After a German victory over Russia in August 1914, fought much closer to Allenstein, Germany named it the Battle of Tannenberg and framed it as revenge for 1410. Nazi Germany portrayed its Lebensraum policies as a continuation of the Order's mission. Soviet historiography styled the battle an ethnic struggle between Slavs and Germans.

Under Communist rule in Poland the state monopolised the battle's memory, and 15 July was an official memorial day until the end of the 1980s. In William Urban's summary, almost all accounts made before the 1960s were more influenced by romantic legend and nationalist propaganda than by fact. Historians have since moved towards dispassionate scholarship.

summary: At Grunwald on 15 July 1410 the Polish and Lithuanian army under Władysław II Jagiełło and Vytautas defeated the Teutonic Order and killed Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen. The Order withstood the siege of Marienburg and lost little land in 1411, but it never regained its former power.
references: Stephen Turnbull, Tannenberg 1410: Disaster for the Teutonic Knights (Osprey, 2003)
Mečislovas Jučas, The Battle of Grünwald (National Museum Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania, 2009)
William Urban, Tannenberg and After: Lithuania, Poland and the Teutonic Order in Search of Immortality (Lithuanian Research and Studies Center, 2003)
Eric Christiansen, The Northern Crusades (Penguin Books, 1997)
Robert Frost, The Oxford History of Poland-Lithuania: The Making of the Polish-Lithuanian Union 1385–1569 (Oxford University Press, 2015)
Stephen M. Kuczynski, The Great War with the Teutonic Knights in the years 1409–1411 (Ministry of National Defence, 1960)
notes: No reliable troop counts exist in the article. I gave Długosz's banner counts and Kuczyński's high-end figures with the article's caveats; the article does not state a total for the Teutonic side beyond Kuczyński's.

Casualty figures are vague and conflicting (8,000 on both sides, possibly 16,000; 18,000 in a papal bull; 203 to 211 of 270 brothers killed). The article says Jagiełło called Polish losses small and Długosz listed 12 knights.

The site is disputed: the traditional site between the three villages versus Ekdahl's site about 2 km south-west; the article says the chapel-area mass graves are, in Ekdahl's view, near the Teutonic camp. The article does not say the graves were Teutonic; I wrote only what it says.

The Lithuanian retreat is disputed (Długosz's rout, a planned manoeuvre, Turnbull's objection). Długosz's own account contradicts Cronica conflictus. The two accounts of von Jungingen's killer are given.

Gilgenburg: the article reports the Order's propaganda that the Polish and Lithuanian army ravaged it, and says mass burials there were found, and that the massacre is known from written sources. It does not say who was responsible; I left the matter out of the text.
The Teutonic Order's claim that von Renys's treason caused the defeat is not in my text for length; the Order beheaded him without trial. The article also says this fed the stab-in-the-back myth.

Left out: Moldavian sword Szczerbiec, Zyndram's claim beyond the doubt, battle flags, names of the Grunwald Swords as a national symbol, memorials' details, and present-day Russian statements of 2014 and 2017.
The dyk says the old-site graves 'probably' lie near the camp, softening Ekdahl's belief as the article gives it; the article says Ekdahl 'believed' this.
